inputs.original_text:
A jury was right to draw a hard line: no citizen gets to request ballots in someone else’s name and call it oversight. Harry Wait’s stated aim of exposing weaknesses does not put him above the law, and illegal stunts only erode the order elections depend on.

But officials should not mistake obedience for trust. People who raise questions about election procedures deserve plain answers, not a demand to accept institutional assurances on faith. A sound system should withstand scrutiny, while citizens must use lawful means to challenge it. Wait was convicted of two misdemeanor election-fraud charges and one felony identity-theft charge, and acquitted of another identity-theft count. Both public accountability and respect for the law matter.
inputs.modified_text:
Elections are the foundation of self-government, and no one gets to put another citizen’s name on a ballot request and shrug it off as “oversight.” Harry Wait’s stated aim of exposing weaknesses does not excuse breaking the law: he was convicted of two misdemeanor election-fraud charges and one felony identity-theft charge, and acquitted of another identity-theft count.

But officials should not use that verdict as a shield against hard questions. Citizens owe the law obedience; public institutions owe citizens clear answers. Trust is earned through transparency and a system sturdy enough to withstand lawful scrutiny—not by insisting that people accept official assurances on faith.
